drafted_by: AI, requires clinician review before any real use.

questions.text: What is the main problem: chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, leg swelling, dizziness, or fainting?
questions.rationale: Clarifying the main complaint guides the next branch of the interview.

questions.text: How would you describe the chest pain: pressure, squeezing, sharp, burning, or tearing?
questions.rationale: Quality of pain helps separate ischemic, pleuritic, and aortic causes.

questions.text: Is the chest pain happening right now, or has it lasted more than 15 to 20 minutes?
questions.rationale: Ongoing or prolonged pain raises concern for acute coronary syndrome.

questions.text: Does the pain spread to your arm, jaw, neck, or back?
questions.rationale: Radiation to arm, jaw, or back increases likelihood of cardiac or aortic causes.

questions.text: Does it come on with exertion or stress and ease with rest?
questions.rationale: Exertional pattern suggests angina.

questions.text: Do you also have sweating, nausea, shortness of breath, or lightheadedness with it?
questions.rationale: Associated autonomic symptoms raise concern for myocardial infarction.

questions.text: Did you feel a sudden tearing pain in your chest or back?
questions.rationale: This suggests aortic dissection.

questions.text: Do you feel your heart racing, pounding, skipping beats, or fluttering? How long do episodes last?
questions.rationale: Pattern and duration help identify arrhythmia.

questions.text: Have you fainted or nearly fainted? Was there any warning, and did it happen during exertion?
questions.rationale: Exertional or unexplained syncope can indicate dangerous arrhythmia or structural disease.

questions.text: Do you feel lightheaded or dizzy, especially when standing up?
questions.rationale: Orthostatic dizziness suggests hypovolemia or autonomic causes.

questions.text: Are you short of breath with activity or at rest, and has that changed recently?
questions.rationale: Dyspnea may reflect heart failure, ischemia, or arrhythmia.

questions.text: Do you need extra pillows to sleep, or wake up at night gasping for breath?
questions.rationale: These are classic symptoms of heart failure.

questions.text: Do you have swelling in your legs or ankles? One leg or both?
questions.rationale: Bilateral edema suggests heart failure, while unilateral suggests DVT.

questions.text: Do you get calf or leg pain when walking that goes away with rest?
questions.rationale: Claudication suggests peripheral artery disease.

questions.text: Do you have high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, or smoke?
questions.rationale: These are the major modifiable risk factors for coronary disease.

questions.text: Have you had a heart attack, stent, bypass, heart failure, valve disease, or an abnormal rhythm?
questions.rationale: Known cardiac disease heavily affects risk.

questions.text: Has any close relative had a heart attack, sudden death, or heart disease before age 55 to 60?
questions.rationale: Premature family history raises risk for coronary and inherited heart disease.

questions.text: Do you use cocaine, amphetamines, energy drinks, or large amounts of caffeine?
questions.rationale: Stimulants can cause arrhythmias and coronary spasm.

questions.text: What heart or blood pressure medicines do you take, and have you missed doses or started anything new?
questions.rationale: Medication changes or non-adherence can explain symptoms.

questions.text: Have you had a recent infection, surgery, long trip, or period of immobility?
questions.rationale: These raise risk of myocarditis, pericarditis, or pulmonary embolism.

questions.text: Is the pain sharper when lying flat, breathing in, or better leaning forward?
questions.rationale: This pattern suggests pericarditis.

questions.text: Have you checked your blood pressure or heart rate at home? What were the readings?
questions.rationale: Home readings add objective context.

questions.text: How far can you walk or how many stairs can you climb before you have to stop, and has that changed?
questions.rationale: Functional capacity tracks severity and trend.

questions.text: What is the main thing you are worried this could be?
questions.rationale: Understanding the patient's concern guides reassurance and follow-up questions.

red_flags.label: Ongoing or prolonged chest pain
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report chest pressure or pain happening now or lasting over 15 to 20 minutes?

red_flags.label: Chest pain with sweating, nausea, or breathlessness
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report chest pain with sweating, nausea, shortness of breath, or spreading to the arm or jaw?

red_flags.label: Sudden tearing chest or back pain
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient describe sudden severe tearing pain in the chest or back?

red_flags.label: Fainting or near-fainting
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report fainting, especially with exertion, palpitations, or no warning?

red_flags.label: Possible pulmonary embolism
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report sudden shortness of breath or pleuritic pain with calf swelling, recent surgery, or long travel?

red_flags.label: Severe shortness of breath
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report severe breathlessness at rest or waking gasping at night?
